Probably a bit dated now, and probably more trivial than you would want, but have you read this post? http://blogs.msdn.com/b/vcblog/archive/2010/08/09/the-filterator.aspx

It wraps an existing iterator, but I think it's still a useful and well-documented example of constructing an iterator.

I think there's a lot of room for improvement in C++'s iterators. I mean, usability-wise it's wonderful, but even though the iterators architecture is extensible, it's not easy at all to extend. It's really important to improve on this.

Also, I realize this has little to do with the question, but a shared_ptr is a form of a global, just so we are clear about this.

Back to iterators. There are a few ways people go about it that I can think of. None of them are as easy as I wish they were, I've already said, but nonetheless. In essence, what you need is

  • Provide a set of typedefs like the standard demands. These tyepdefs allow standard algorithms to work with any iterator, and they also allow algorithms to be as efficient as possible had you done the same with explicit none-template C++ code, C code, assembly or machine code. For example, the std::advance() algorithm advances an iterator n steps; the same algorithm will work on std::list<>::iterator and std::array<>::iterator, and will be correct and efficient either way, thanks to the typedefs (and in particular the iterator_category typedef).
  • Provide functionality (functions, some members, others free) as dictated by the iterator category. For example, an input iterator requires the increment functionality, so you must provide the operator++() and operator++(int) members; whereas a random access iterator requires that as well as indexing, so you must provide operator[]().

That's it. Typedefs and functions. EVerything and anything else is up to you. You don't have to derive from anything, but you may if you choose to. You don't have to have data in the iterator struct, but you may if you choose to. As far as standard algorithms are concerned, if it feels to them like an iterator, it is an iterator. And it feels like an iterator when it has the typedefs and it has the functionality guaranteed by the iterator's category.

So, approaches I can think of for defining a custom iterator:

  • Write the iterator from scratch, keystroke by keystroke. It's a wonderful exercise to reveal some of the challenges the architecture poses on ease of extensibility. I mean, if you go this way, you'll see what other approaches try and help you with, and maybe why they only go as far as they do.
  • Derive from std::iterator<>. I frankly have yet to do this myself. The iterator class is "meant" to be a base class for iterators, but actually takes more work than deriving from std::iterator_traits, which coincidentally was never meant for deriving. I'm not sure what the difference is between std::iterator and std::iterator_traits; I think they essentially provide the same set of typedefs, and nothing else. But it turns out that if you wish to create a custom iterator that is a wrapper for an existing iterator, then it's easier to ...
  • Derive from std::iterator_traits<>. This is a standard traits class, coming with a set of typedefs and nothing else. It is specialized on pointers, expressing that pointers are iterators, and also on any type that is an iterator, forwarding the typedefs to the type's typedefs. So for example, std::iterator_traits<std::list<std::string>::iterator> defines its value_type typedef as typename std::list<std::string>::iterator::value_type. The std::list<std::string>::iterator then explicitly adds a typedef for value_type, to be std::string. So, all this to say, that in practice if you create a custom iterator that is a wrapper for another iterator--say--a std::list<std::string>::iterator--then to save the work of adding the necessary typedefs to your class it's easiest to derive from std::iterator_traits<std::list<std::string>::iterator>>, because you then get the typedefs for free. In fact, if you wrap any iterator, that's one way to go: template<typename Iter> struct custom_iterator : std::iterator_traits<Iter> { /*...*/ };
  • Use the Boost.Iterator library. The Boost Iterator library has an iterator facade that eases writing custom iterators. It's not standard, but any self-respecting C++ developer will have Boost set up on their development environment.

In practice I think that people often choose an approach depending on the case. They'd often take the Boost path either way, but sometimes they'd take the std::iterator_traits derivative if they wrap another iterator, or a from-scratch or a std::iterator derivative if they don't merely wrap another iterator.

As for the ranged for-loop, I don't think this matters. The ranged-for loop is guaranteed to work on anything on which ADLed begin() and end() yield iterators. So, for(auto const& e : container) works so long as begin(container) and end(container) yield iterators pointing at the beginning and end of the container.

Finally, I think things are going to change. We've got ranges around the corner, and this is a whole new game. It changes the iterator architecture, and from what I see in Eric Niebler's Range-v3 library, which reflects his ranges proposal, this will be beautiful -- at least from a usability perspective... I'm not sure yet about extensibility; haven't tried writing my own range yet. :) I think a range is essentially a type that expresses ... well, a range. So a begin and an end. I hope the committee will take the opportunity to try and improve on the ease of extensibility here too.

Good luck!

Linux distros don't matter that much since they are easy to reinstall and customize once you get the hang of linux so don't be afraid to experiment.
